speaker_role: independent counselor (Director of College Counseling at Phillips Academy)
commercial_incentive: None evident; appears to be an educational interview series.
key_insights: Explains the FAFSA is free, income/asset-driven, and produces an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) that colleges use to build an aid package by subtracting EFC from cost of attendance.
Advises completing the FAFSA as soon as parents' taxes are filed, noting a college's financial aid deadline can matter even more than its admission deadline when aid funds are limited.

Explains the CSS Profile (College Board) is a paid, more detailed form some mostly-private colleges require in addition to FAFSA, examining both biological parents' finances even after divorce and additional assets like home equity.
Notes CSS Profile fee waivers exist for lower-income families, and CSS opens earlier than FAFSA in the fall, letting schools give preliminary aid estimates alongside early decision/action results.
States a typical aid package combines grants/scholarships (no repayment), loans (repaid later), and work-study (earned during the school year, roughly 8-20 hours per week).
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says most colleges want the FAFSA submitted between February 1st and mid-March (dated guidance).
Speaker says a FAFSA filer could historically list only 10 schools at a time before needing to swap entries.
notable_or_distinctive: Clear, simple two-form (FAFSA vs CSS Profile) comparison framework, though delivered in a now-outdated interview format.
reliability_notes: Video is roughly 12 years old; FAFSA opening/filing dates, the EFC terminology (since replaced by the Student Aid Index), and the 10-school limit have since changed, so viewers should verify current rules rather than rely on this video's specifics.
